q.q: Who created Scratch?
o: The BBC as part of the micro:bit project
Microsoft as part of Visual Studio
The Lifelong Kindergarten group at the MIT Media Lab
The Raspberry Pi Foundation in Cambridge
q.why: Scratch was made by the Lifelong Kindergarten group at the MIT Media Lab and first released in 2007.

q.q: What is the stage in Scratch?
o: The list of blocks sorted into categories
The space where blocks are joined into scripts
The area where the project runs and sprites appear
The tab used to draw a sprite's costumes
q.why: The stage, top right, is where the project is shown running.

q.q: What is a script in Scratch?
o: A single block dragged from the blocks palette
A stack of joined blocks that runs from top to bottom
A picture that a sprite can switch to
A background image shown on the stage
q.why: A script is a stack of blocks joined together.

q.q: What is the blocks palette?
o: The area where the sprites move about and talk
The list of blocks in the chosen category, ready to drag
The panel showing a sprite's x, y and size
The menu used to save and load projects
q.why: The palette shows the blocks you can drag into the scripts area.

q.q: Ellie clicks on the Dog sprite and the scripts she built for the Cat disappear. What has happened?
o: Clicking a new sprite deletes the other sprite's scripts
Her scripts have been moved onto the stage instead
Each sprite has its own scripts, so she now sees the Dog's
The Cat's scripts only show while the project runs
q.why: The scripts area shows the scripts of the selected sprite only.

q.q: In which category would you find the [repeat (10)] block?
o: Motion
Events
Control
Operators
q.why: Loops, waits and if blocks are in the orange Control category.

q.q: Which part of Scratch would you use to give a quiz a classroom picture behind everything?
o: A backdrop on the stage
A costume on a sprite
A block in the palette
A message broadcast
q.why: Background pictures for the stage are backdrops.

q.q: Which block category holds [say (Hello!) for (2) seconds]?
o: Sound
Looks
Events
Sensing
q.why: Speech bubbles, costumes and size are Looks blocks.

q.q: What is an event in Scratch?
o: Something that happens, such as a key press, that starts a script
A block that repeats the blocks inside it
A named store that holds a value
A picture shown behind the sprites
q.why: Events such as clicking the flag or pressing a key start scripts.

q.q: What does sequence mean in programming?
o: Instructions are repeated a set number of times
The program chooses which instructions to run
Instructions are sent as messages to every sprite
Instructions are carried out one after another in order
q.why: Sequence: one after another, top to bottom.

q.q: Where must a hat block such as [when green flag clicked] go?
o: At the bottom of a script
At the top of a script
Inside a repeat loop
Inside an if block
q.why: Hat blocks have a curved top and start scripts.

q.q: Which block starts a script when the user clicks on that sprite?
o: [when this sprite clicked]
[when green flag clicked]
[when I receive (click)]
[when (space) key pressed]
q.why: When this sprite clicked responds to a mouse click on the sprite.

q.q: A sprite should walk to the door and then say 'Knock knock'. The script has the say block above the move block. What happens?
o: It walks to the door and then says 'Knock knock'
It says nothing because the order is not allowed
It says 'Knock knock' before it walks to the door
It walks and speaks at exactly the same moment
q.why: Blocks run top to bottom, so the speech comes first.

q.q: What is the difference between [say (Hi!)] and [say (Hi!) for (2) seconds]?
o: Only the second one makes the script wait
Only the first one makes the script wait
Only the second one shows a speech bubble
Only the first one can be used with the flag
q.why: The 'for 2 seconds' version waits before the next block runs.

q.q: Why is it good to start a green flag script with [go to x: (0) y: (0)]?
o: The sprite moves faster for the rest of the game
The script cannot run without a go to block
It stops other sprites moving into the centre
The sprite starts in the same place every time
q.why: Resetting the position makes every run start the same way.

q.q: A script has [say (3)], [say (2)], [say (1)], [say (Go!)] with nothing else. What does the user see?
o: 3, 2, 1 then Go!, one second apart
Only 'Go!', because the blocks run too fast to see
3 only, as later say blocks are ignored
Nothing, because say needs a time added
q.why: Plain say blocks do not wait, so each is replaced instantly.

q.q: What is the x range of the Scratch stage?
q.why: The stage is 480 steps wide, from -240 on the left to 240 on the right.

q.q: What are the coordinates of the bottom-right corner of the stage?
q.why: Right edge x = 240, bottom edge y = -180.

q.q: Which way does a sprite face after [point in direction (180)]?
o: Up
Left
Down
Right
q.why: 180 is down, 0 is up, 90 is right and -90 is left.

q.q: A sprite is at (30, -40). It runs [change x by (-50)]. Where is it now?
q.why: Only x changes: 30 - 50 = -20.

q.q: A sprite is at (-60, 70). It runs [change y by (-100)] then [change x by (60)]. Where is it now?
A sprite at (0, 0) faces up and runs [move (40) steps]. Where is it?
q.why: Facing up, moving adds to y.

q.q: A sprite at (0, 0) facing right runs [move (50) steps], [turn ↺ (90) degrees], [move (20) steps]. Where does it finish?
q.why: Right 50 to (50, 0); turning anticlockwise makes it face up; up 20 gives (50, 20).

q.q: Every time the right arrow is pressed, a sprite should move right, but it jumps to x = 10 and stays there. Which block was used by mistake?
o: [set x to (10)]
[change x by (10)]
[move (10) steps]
[change y by (10)]
q.why: Set always puts it at the same x; change adds to x.

q.q: Which block would make a sprite fall down the stage a little each time it runs?
o: [change y by (-5)]
[change y by (5)]
[change x by (-5)]
[set y to (-5)]
q.why: Negative change in y moves a sprite down.

q.q: Why does [move (10) steps] sometimes move a sprite left instead of right?
o: It always moves left when x is negative
It chooses a random direction each time
It moves left whenever it touches a sprite
It moves in whichever direction the sprite is facing
q.why: Move steps follows the sprite's direction.

q.q: What is animation in Scratch?
o: Changing the backdrop once at the start
Moving a sprite to an exact x and y position
Playing a sound until it has finished
Switching quickly between slightly different costumes
q.why: Showing changing pictures quickly looks like movement.

q.q: What does [next costume] do when the sprite is already on its last costume?
o: Stops on the last costume for good
Hides the sprite from the stage
Shows an error in the scripts area
Goes back to the first costume
q.why: Next costume wraps round to the first.

q.q: Which wait is most likely to give a smooth walking animation?
o: [wait (2) seconds]
[wait (5) seconds]
[wait (0) seconds]
[wait (0.2) seconds]
q.why: About 0.1 to 0.3 seconds lets each costume be seen without being jerky.

q.q: A game hides its player at game over. When the flag is clicked again the player is missing. What is the best fix?
o: Add [show] to the green flag script
Add [hide] to the green flag script
Add [next costume] to the game over script
Add [wait (1) seconds] before the hide
q.why: Hidden sprites stay hidden until a show block runs.

q.q: A sprite at size 100% runs [set size to (50) %] then [change size by (20)]. What size is it?
q.why: Set to 50, then add 20: 70%.

q.q: A pop sound should play while the game carries on straight away. Which block is best?
o: [play sound (pop) until done]
[stop all sounds]
[change volume by (10)]
[start sound (pop)]
q.why: Start sound does not make the script wait.

q.q: In which tab do you draw or edit a sprite's costumes?
o: Costumes
Code
Sounds
Backdrops
q.why: The Costumes tab holds the paint editor and costume list.

q.q: What is iteration?
o: Repeating instructions using a loop
Choosing between two sets of instructions
Running instructions in order, top to bottom
Storing a value that can change
q.why: Iteration means repeating instructions, usually with a loop.

q.q: Which type of loop is [repeat until <touching (edge)?>]?
o: Count-controlled
Condition-controlled
Event-controlled
Sequence-controlled
q.why: It stops when a condition becomes true.

q.q: Which loop runs until the red stop sign is clicked?
o: [repeat (100)]
[forever]
[repeat until <(score) = (10)>]
[wait until <key (space) pressed?>]
q.why: Forever never finishes by itself.

q.q: Why can no block be attached underneath a [forever] block?
o: It never finishes, so a block under it would never run
Scratch only allows one forever block per sprite
Forever must always be the last block in the palette
Blocks under forever would run before the loop
q.why: Forever is a cap block because the loop never ends.

q.q: What turn is needed inside [repeat (8)] to draw a regular octagon?
o: 40 degrees
60 degrees
135 degrees
45 degrees
q.why: Turn angle = 360 / number of sides = 360 / 8 = 45 degrees.

q.q: A loop [repeat (6)] contains [move (30) steps] and [turn ↻ (60) degrees]. What does it draw with the pen down?
o: A regular pentagon with sides of 30
A regular hexagon with sides of 30
A regular hexagon with sides of 60
A triangle with sides of 30
q.why: 6 sides, turning 360 / 6 = 60 degrees each time.

q.q: When is a condition-controlled loop a better choice than a count-controlled loop?
o: When you know exactly how many times to repeat
When the blocks should only ever run once
When you want the loop to run for ever
When you know when to stop but not how many times
q.why: Repeat until stops on a condition, however many repeats that takes.

q.q: A [repeat (3)] loop contains a [repeat (5)] loop with [next costume] inside. How many times does [next costume] run?
q.why: 5 times for each of the 3 outer repeats: 15.

q.q: Ben puts [next costume] directly under a [repeat (10)] block instead of inside it. What happens?
o: The costume changes ten times as he wanted
The costume never changes at all
The costume changes only once, after the loop
Scratch moves the block inside the loop
q.why: Blocks after a loop run once, when the loop ends.

q.q: Which is the main advantage of a loop over copying blocks?
o: The project always runs at least twice as fast
Fewer blocks, so it is easier to read and change
Loops stop sprites going off the edge
Loops are the only way to use the pen
q.why: Loops make scripts shorter, clearer and easier to edit.

q.q: What does an [if <> then else] block do?
o: Repeats its blocks until the condition is true
Runs one set of blocks if true and another if false
Runs its blocks only when the flag is clicked
Runs both sets of blocks one after the other
q.why: If-else chooses between two paths.

q.q: What can a Boolean block report?
o: Any whole number
Only true or false
Any text the user types
A sprite's x and y position
q.why: Booleans are true or false.

q.q: Which block gives the text the user typed after an ask block?
o: (timer)
(username)
(costume number)
(answer)
q.why: Answer holds the reply to the last ask.

q.q: Which sensing block could tell if a maze sprite has hit a black wall?
o: <key (black) pressed?>
<mouse down?>
<touching colour (black)?>
(distance to (mouse-pointer))
q.why: Touching colour checks for a colour on the stage.

q.q: A quiz asks 'What is 9 × 6?' and checks <(answer) = (54)>. A pupil types 56. What runs?
o: The top part, because the answer is close
Both parts, one after the other
Neither part, as 56 is not allowed
The else part, because the condition is false
q.why: 56 is not equal to 54, so the condition is false.

q.q: Why is an [if <key (right arrow) pressed?> then] block usually placed inside [forever]?
o: So it only checks the key once at the start
So the arrow key cannot be pressed twice
So the sprite always moves right forever
So it keeps checking the key the whole time
q.why: An if checks once when it runs; forever makes it check again and again.

q.q: In Scratch, is <(answer) = (Enniskillen)> true if the user types ENNISKILLEN?
o: No, capital letters must match exactly
Yes, Scratch's = ignores capital letters
No, because answer always holds a number
Yes, but only if the timer is reset first
q.why: Scratch's equals block is not case-sensitive.

q.q: A game should say Gold for a score over 20, Silver for over 10 and Bronze otherwise. What is the best structure?
o: Three separate repeat loops, one per medal
An if-else with another if-else in its else part
One if block with no else part at all
A forever loop holding one say block
q.why: Nested if-else handles more than two choices.

q.q: What does [ask (What is your name?) and wait] do?
o: Says the question for two seconds and moves on
Picks a random name from a list
Broadcasts the question to every sprite
Shows a box and waits for the user to type
q.why: Ask shows an input box and waits for a reply.

q.q: Which block adds 1 to the current value of score?
o: [set (score) to (1)]
[change (score) by (1)]
[show variable (score)]
q.why: Change adds to the current value; set replaces it.

q.q: Which data type is best for storing a player's name?
o: Integer
Boolean
String
Float
q.why: Text is stored as a string.

q.q: Which data type is best for a timer that shows 12.5 seconds?
o: Float
Integer
Boolean
String
q.why: Numbers with a decimal point are floats (real numbers).

q.q: What does (pick random (1) to (10)) report?
o: A whole number from 2 to 9 only
A whole number from 1 to 10, including 1 and 10
A decimal number between 0 and 1
The numbers 1 and 10 only
q.why: Both end values are included.

q.q: score starts at 0. The script runs [change (score) by (5)] three times, then [change (score) by (-2)]. What is score?
lives is 3. The script runs [set (lives) to ((lives) * (2))] then [change (lives) by (-1)]. What is lives?
What does <(7) > (12)> report?
o: true
false
q.why: 7 is not greater than 12, so it reports false.

q.q: What does (join (Lough) (Erne)) report?
o: LoughErne
Lough Erne
Lough + Erne
ErneLough
q.why: Join sticks the text together with no space unless you add one.

q.q: How could you check 'score is 10 or more' for whole-number scores in Scratch?
q.why: Scratch has no greater-than-or-equal block; above 9 means 10 or more for whole numbers.

q.q: Why should [set (lives) to (3)] go under [when green flag clicked]?
o: So the player loses a life every second
So the lives variable is hidden
So every new game starts with 3 lives
So lives can never go below 3
q.why: Resetting variables at the start stops old values carrying over.

q.q: What does [broadcast (start game)] do?
o: Sends a message to one chosen sprite only
Starts the green flag scripts again
Shows 'start game' in a speech bubble
Sends a message to every sprite and the stage
q.why: Broadcasts go to everyone.

q.q: Which block runs a script when the message 'level 2' arrives?
o: [broadcast (level 2)]
[switch backdrop to (level 2)]
[when backdrop switches to (level 1)]
[when I receive (level 2)]
q.why: When I receive is the hat block for a message.

q.q: A Start button broadcasts 'start'. Three sprites have [when I receive (start)]. How many of their scripts run?
o: Only the first sprite made
Only the sprite nearest the button
None until the green flag is clicked
All three, at the same time
q.why: Every matching receive script starts.

q.q: One sprite broadcasts 'Game Over ' with a space at the end. Another waits for 'Game Over'. Why might nothing happen?
o: Broadcasts cannot contain capital letters
The message names do not match exactly
Only the stage can receive messages
Messages only work inside a forever loop
q.why: Message names must match; pick from the drop-down to avoid typos.

q.q: What does [broadcast (show results) and wait] do that [broadcast (show results)] does not?
o: Waits until the receiving scripts have finished
Waits one second before sending the message
Sends the message to the stage only
Sends the message again until it is received
q.why: The 'and wait' version pauses the sender.

q.q: Why is putting [broadcast (hit)] alone inside [forever] a bad idea?
o: It sends the message again and again, restarting scripts
It sends the message only once and then stops
Broadcast blocks cannot be put inside loops
It makes every sprite hide straight away
q.why: Receiving scripts keep restarting and never finish.

q.q: The school intercom is a good comparison for a broadcast. Why?
o: Only one class can hear each announcement
One announcement reaches everyone, and each acts on it
Every class must reply before it continues
Announcements are only made at the start of the day
q.why: A broadcast is sent to all; only those concerned react.

q.q: What is a My Block?
o: A custom block you define once and use many times
A block that only works on the stage
A block that starts a script when a key is pressed
A variable that only one sprite can use
q.why: My Blocks are custom blocks made with Make a Block.

q.q: Making a block called 'reset game' that holds eight set and go to blocks is an example of...
o: Abstraction
Iteration
Selection
Broadcasting
q.why: The detail is hidden behind a simple name.

q.q: Under which hat block do you put the blocks that a My Block will run?
o: [when green flag clicked]
[when I receive (block name)]
[define (block name)]
[when this sprite clicked]
q.why: The define block holds the custom block's instructions.

q.q: A My Block is [define square (size)] with [repeat (4)] containing [move (size) steps] and [turn ↻ (90) degrees]. What does [square (25)] draw?
o: A square with sides of 100
25 squares of size 4
A square with sides of 25
A square with sides of 90
q.why: size = 25, so each side is 25 steps.

q.q: [define draw shape (sides) (size)] turns 360 / sides degrees. What turn does [draw shape (10) (20)] make?
o: 18 degrees
20 degrees
36 degrees
72 degrees
q.why: sides = 10, so the turn is 360 / 10 = 36 degrees.

q.q: What is an input of a custom block called in C#?
o: A costume
A condition
A parameter
A broadcast
q.why: Inputs to functions are parameters.

q.q: A bug is found in a 'jump' My Block used in six places. How many places need fixing?
o: Six: every place it is used
One: the define script
Seven: the define and every use
None: My Blocks cannot have bugs
q.why: Fix the definition once and every use is fixed.

q.q: The Cat has a My Block called 'jump'. Can the Dog sprite use it straight away?
o: Yes, every sprite gets every My Block
No, a My Block belongs to the sprite it was made in
Yes, but only if it is broadcast first
No, My Blocks only work on the stage
q.why: My Blocks are local to their sprite unless copied.

q.q: What is a simulation?
o: Running a model to see what happens over time
An exact copy of every detail of a real system
A picture of a real place used as a backdrop
A loop that repeats exactly ten times
q.why: A simulation runs a model.

q.q: Why are models simplified?
o: They keep only the parts that matter for the question
Computers cannot store any detailed information
Simplified models always give perfect predictions
Scratch only allows two variables per project
q.why: Simplifying makes a model easier to build, at the cost of accuracy.

q.q: A population of 10 doubles every year. How many after 3 years?
q.why: Doubling each year: 10, then 20, then 40, then 80.

q.q: 100 rabbits grow by 50% a year. How many after 2 years?
In the bouncing ball model, gravity is changed from -1 to -3. What happens?
o: The ball falls more slowly and gently
The ball stops bouncing at all
The ball speeds up much faster as it falls
The ball moves sideways instead
q.why: A bigger negative gravity changes speed more each moment.

q.q: The ball's bounce uses [set (speed) to ((speed) * (-0.5))]. What kind of ball does this model?
o: A ball that loses half its speed each bounce
A ball that bounces higher every time
A ball that never leaves the ground
A ball that bounces at exactly the same height
q.why: Multiplying by -0.5 reverses it and keeps half its speed.

q.q: A rabbit model predicts millions of rabbits on a small island after 30 years. What is the best reason to doubt it?
o: Scratch cannot work out large numbers
The growth rate variable was too small
It leaves out limits such as food and space
Models can only run for a few years
q.why: Missing factors stop real populations growing for ever.

q.q: What is a logic error?
o: The program runs but does the wrong thing
The program will not run at all because of a typo
The computer runs out of memory
The sprite has the wrong costume name
q.why: Logic errors give wrong results without crashing.

q.q: What is tracing a script?
o: Drawing round a sprite with the pen
Copying a script from another project
Deleting blocks until the bug goes away
Stepping through it block by block, tracking variables
q.why: Tracing follows the program as the computer would.

q.q: Nothing happens when the green flag is clicked. Which is the most likely cause?
o: The script uses a repeat block inside it
The sprite has more than one costume
The script has no [when green flag clicked] on top
The stage has a backdrop selected
q.why: Without a hat block the script never starts.

q.q: [set (n) to (1)] then [repeat (4)] containing [set (n) to ((n) * (2))]. What is n at the end?
q.why: n doubles four times: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

q.q: A script should count 1 to 3 but says 0, 1, 2. Inside the loop, say comes before change. What is the fix?
o: Change repeat (3) to repeat (4)
Put the change block above the say block
Set count to -1 at the start
Use [forever] instead of [repeat (3)]
q.why: Changing before saying makes it say 1, 2, 3.

q.q: Points go up by 2 each time, from 1. Why does [repeat until <(points) = (10)>] never stop?
o: Points can never be larger than 9
Points go 9 then 11, never exactly 10
Repeat until can only check text
A loop cannot use the = operator
q.why: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11: never equal to 10.

q.q: Why should you change only one thing at a time when debugging?
o: Because Scratch only saves one change at a time
Because changing two blocks deletes the sprite
So that the project runs more quickly
So you know which change fixed or broke it
q.why: Testing after each small change shows its effect.

q.q: Which is a useful way to watch a variable change while a game runs?
o: Hide it using [hide variable]
Rename it to something shorter
Move it to a different sprite
Tick its box to show it on the stage
q.why: Showing a variable lets you watch its value.

q.q: Why are syntax errors rare in Scratch compared with C#?
o: Blocks only snap together in valid ways
Scratch programs never contain any mistakes
Scratch checks spelling as you type each command
Scratch has no loops, variables or conditions
q.why: Block shapes prevent most spelling and bracket errors.

q.q: What is the correct order of the development cycle?
o: Plan, develop, test, refine
Develop, test, plan, refine
Plan, refine, develop, test
Test, develop, plan, refine
q.why: Plan, then build, then test, then improve, and repeat.

q.q: Which part of a user story says WHY the user wants something?
o: The 'As a' part
The 'so that' part
The 'I want' part
The 'expected result' part
q.why: As a (who), I want (what), so that (why).

q.q: Which test is erroneous test data for a catch game controlled by arrow keys?
o: Holding the right arrow
Catching an apple
Pressing the space bar
Losing the last life
q.why: Erroneous data is input the program should not normally get.

q.q: A test's expected result is 'lives = 2' but the actual result is 'lives = 3'. What should go in the pass/fail column?
o: Pass
Fail
Boundary
Normal
q.why: Actual did not match expected.

q.q: Who should a game designer think about first, using user-centred design?
o: The people who will play the game
The programmer's own favourite colours
Whichever sprite is easiest to draw
How many blocks the project will use
q.why: User-centred design starts from the users' needs.

q.q: Why is it better to build and test one feature at a time?
o: Bugs are easier to find in a small new part
Scratch can only save one feature
Testing is only allowed at the very end
It means no testing is needed later
q.why: Small steps make it clear where a bug came from.

q.q: Which of these is a refinement made after watching a P2 pupil play?
o: Writing the first user story for the game
Choosing which sprites the game will need
Filling in the expected results column
Replacing written instructions with pictures
q.why: Refining improves the product using feedback.
